title: New Jersey EMT
summary: The New Jersey layer on top of the national EMT curriculum: how NJ certifies you, what the 2025 statewide protocols actually let an EMT do, the NJ drug list, refusal and DNR rules, where South Jersey patients go, and what the PA practice act says about the job you are aiming at.

lessons.title: How New Jersey certifies an EMT
lessons.body:
Two different organizations have a say in whether you can work on an ambulance in New Jersey. The **National Registry of Emergency Medical Technicians (NREMT)** writes and scores the cognitive exam. The **New Jersey Office of Emergency Medical Services (OEMS)**, inside the NJ Department of Health, issues the card that actually lets you practice here. Passing NREMT does not by itself make you a New Jersey EMT.

The rules live in the New Jersey Administrative Code, Chapter 8:40A (`N.J.A.C. 8:40A`), "Emergency Medical Technicians-Basics: Training and Certification." Source: NJ DOH OEMS, https://www.nj.gov/health/ems/documents/reg-enforcement/njac840ar.pdf

## Getting the card the first time

`N.J.A.C. 8:40A-7.2` lists three requirements: you must be at least `18`, hold a current CPR certification, and finish an approved EMT-Basic training program that includes a `10-hour` clinical experience, then pass the NREMT-Basic certification examination.

If you turn 18 after the exam, the rule has a bridge. `8:40A-7.4` gives minors who pass the NREMT assessment exam **provisional** status only: they work in the physical presence and under direct supervision of a certified EMT and cannot be counted toward the minimum crew on an ambulance.

Your first card is valid for **not less than 36 and not more than 42 months**.

> **Key:** NREMT is the exam. OEMS is the license. You need both, and only OEMS can discipline your NJ practice.

## Coming in from another state

`8:40A-7.3` is the reciprocity rule, and it is unusually specific. Someone validly certified by the NREMT, by New York, or by an Atlantic EMS Council member state (Delaware, DC, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Virginia, West Virginia) already has status as an EMT-Basic in NJ. To get an actual NJ card, an out-of-state holder completes a reciprocity application and an approved **Core 13** program; the non-NREMT states also need a certificate of eligibility and a passing score on the NREMT assessment exam.

That matters in South Jersey, where Philadelphia is a twenty-minute drive. A Pennsylvania EMT is not automatically carrying a NJ card.

## Staying certified

`8:40A-7.5` sets the recertification arithmetic: **24 core credit hours plus 24 elective credit hours**, `48` total, accrued over the **36-month period immediately before** recertification. The 24 core hours are two hours from each of the 12 core sessions listed at `8:40A-9.5(a)1i`, or one approved Core 13 program instead.

Credits do not carry forward. At the start of each new cycle the balance resets to zero core and zero elective. OEMS mails a CEU status letter about six months before your card expires, free of charge.

Let it lapse and `8:40A-7.6` applies: a Core 13 program **and** a passing score on the NREMT-Basic certification exam again. There is no quiet grace period.

> **On shift:** Log CEUs the week you earn them. The rule counts hours in the 36 months before renewal, so a class you took 40 months ago is worth nothing.
keyPoints: NREMT gives the exam; NJ OEMS issues the certification card under N.J.A.C. 8:40A.
Initial certification: age 18, current CPR, approved program with a 10-hour clinical, pass NREMT.
Cards are valid 36 to 42 months; recert needs 24 core plus 24 elective CEU hours in the prior 36 months.
CEUs never carry forward between cycles.
Expired certification means Core 13 plus retaking the NREMT-Basic certification exam.

checks.q: How many total continuing education hours does N.J.A.C. 8:40A-7.5 require for EMT-Basic recertification, and over what window?
choices: 24 hours over 24 months
48 hours over the prior 36 months
72 hours over the prior 48 months
40 hours over the prior 12 months
checks.why: The rule requires 24 core plus 24 elective credit hours, 48 total, accrued in the 36-month period immediately before recertification.

checks.q: A 17-year-old passes the NREMT assessment exam in New Jersey. What is their status?
choices: Full EMT-Basic certification
Provisional status, working only under direct supervision and not counted toward minimum crew
No status until they retake the exam at 18
Certified but limited to non-emergency transport
checks.why: N.J.A.C. 8:40A-7.4 grants minors provisional status only; full certification is issued at age 18 if all 8:40A-7.2 requirements are met.

checks.q: An EMT lets their NJ card expire by four months. What does N.J.A.C. 8:40A-7.6 require?
choices: Pay a late fee and submit missing CEUs
Complete a Core 13 program and pass the NREMT-Basic certification exam again
Nothing; cards have a six-month grace period
Complete 12 elective hours only
checks.why: Expired certification is treated as a fresh start: an approved Core 13 program plus a passing NREMT-Basic certification exam score. There is no fee-only fix.

lessons.title: How the NJ statewide protocols are built
lessons.body:
Your textbook teaches assessment and pathophysiology. It does not tell you what you are allowed to do on a New Jersey ambulance. That comes from the **New Jersey EMS Clinical Practice Protocols and Guidelines**, version 1, dated **8/21/2025**, published by NJ DOH OEMS at https://www.nj.gov/health/ems/documents/NEWJERSEYEMSCLINICALPRACTICEPROTOCOLS_GUIDELINES_FINAL8.21.2025v1.pdf

This is a `248-page` document covering both BLS and ALS. New Jersey adopted it from the Vermont EMS protocol set, with permission, and its Mobile Intensive Care Advisory Committee edited it to match New Jersey scope of practice.

## The layout you need to recognize

Every protocol is numbered by section: `1` General Patient Care, `2` Medical, `3` Cardiac, `4` Trauma, `5` Airway, `6` Medical Procedures, `7` Prerequisite, `8` Medical Policies, `9` Hazmat and MCI. A suffix of `A` or `P` means adult or pediatric (`2.8A` hypoglycemia adult, `2.8P` pediatric). No suffix means the protocol covers both.

Inside each protocol the steps are grouped under headings: **EMT** first, then **PARAMEDIC & MICN**, then sometimes **COMMUNICATION FAILURE**. Your job is the EMT block. Everything below it tells you what the medic will do when they arrive, which is why reading the whole page makes you a better partner.

> **Key:** Standing orders are cumulative. A paramedic's standing orders include everything authorized at lower levels, and any clinician may switch or combine protocols as the patient changes.

## Four rules the document states outright

1. A medical director may **restrict, but not expand**, your scope of practice. Your agency can decide you do not carry albuterol. It cannot decide you push dextrose.
2. "Call for ALS intercept" appears wherever a paramedic could do something an EMT cannot. It is a prompt, not a delay: several protocols say do not wait.
3. Standing orders are treatments you may start without calling. Anything beyond standing orders requires on-line **medical command**, and medical command may not authorize a procedure outside your defined scope.
4. Clinical judgment is explicitly permitted. The protocols say you may deviate from the order of operations when the patient's presentation calls for it, unless a specific protocol says otherwise.

## Where the national curriculum and NJ diverge

National education standards describe competencies. New Jersey regulation, `N.J.A.C. 8:40A-10.1(b)`, lists actual authorized skills, and that list is older than the education standards it points at. OEMS closed the gap with a waiver rather than a rule change, which is why some NJ EMTs carry albuterol and CPAP and some do not.

> **Trap:** "It is in my textbook" and "it is in the NJ protocol" are different claims, and "my agency is approved for it" is a third. All three have to line up before you do the skill.
keyPoints: The governing document is the NJ EMS Clinical Practice Protocols and Guidelines v1, 8/21/2025, from NJ DOH OEMS.
Protocols are numbered by section with A/P suffixes for adult and pediatric versions.
Each protocol lists EMT steps first, then Paramedic and MICN, then communication failure.
A medical director may restrict but never expand your scope.
Standing orders are cumulative; anything beyond them requires on-line medical command.

checks.q: In the NJ protocols, what does a protocol number ending in 'P' indicate, such as 2.8P?
choices: Paramedic-only protocol
The pediatric version of that protocol
A protocol requiring medical command
A procedure rather than a treatment protocol
checks.why: A and P suffixes mark adult and pediatric versions of the same protocol. Paramedic steps are marked by heading inside each protocol, not by the number.

checks.q: Your agency medical director tells you the agency will not carry oral glucose. Is that allowed?
choices: No, statewide protocols override agency decisions
Yes, a medical director may restrict but not expand scope
Only with OEMS written approval
Only if the agency is a volunteer squad
checks.why: The 2025 protocols state medical directors may restrict, but not expand, the scope of practice at each provider level. Restriction is permitted; expansion is not.

checks.q: What does the protocol phrase 'Call for ALS intercept' mean for an EMT?
choices: Stop treatment and wait on scene for the medic
Request paramedic help because a paramedic can do something beyond EMT scope
Contact medical command for permission
Transfer care and clear the call
checks.why: The preface explains the phrase flags clinical situations where paramedic-level assessment or intervention would benefit the patient. Several protocols explicitly say not to delay transport for it.

lessons.title: The New Jersey EMT drug list
lessons.body:
Two documents decide what you can give. `N.J.A.C. 8:40A-10.1(b)` is the baseline scope rule. The **EMT Scope of Practice waiver dated June 24, 2024** adds to it. The 2025 protocols then supply the doses.

## The baseline: assisting, not administering

`8:40A-10.1(b)` authorizes oxygen administration and, at item 13, **assisting a patient to administer drugs previously prescribed for that patient**, limited to a prescribed metered dose inhaler, sublingual nitroglycerin, and an epinephrine auto-injector. Read the verb: the baseline rule is written around the patient's own medication.

Source: https://www.nj.gov/health/ems/documents/reg-enforcement/njac840ar.pdf

## What the 2025 protocols authorize under the EMT heading

| Drug | NJ EMT dose as published | Protocol |
|---|---|---|
| Oxygen | titrate to `SpO2 94%` or above; `90%` acceptable in COPD | 3.0, 2.12A |
| Aspirin | `324 mg` PO chewable; if patient already took `81 mg`, give the remaining `243 mg` | 3.0 ACS Adult |
| Nitroglycerin | facilitate the **patient's own** nitroglycerin every `3-5 min` while symptoms persist and systolic BP stays at or above `100 mmHg`, to a total of `3` doses | 3.0 ACS Adult |
| Epinephrine auto-injector, adult | `0.3 mg IM`, anterolateral thigh preferred; repeat dosing requires medical command | 2.2 Anaphylaxis Adult |
| Epinephrine auto-injector, pediatric | the age and weight appropriate `0.15 mg` auto-injector | 2.2P Anaphylaxis Pediatric |
| Naloxone, adult | nasal spray `4 mg` into one nostril, **or** `1 mg (1 mL)` per nostril by atomizer to a maximum of `4 mg`; may repeat the initial dose after `5 min` | 2.3A Altered Mental Status Adult |
| Oral glucose, adult | `1-2` tubes of commercial glucose gel; patient must be alert enough to swallow and protect the airway | 2.8A Hypoglycemia Adult |
| Oral glucose, pediatric | `0.5 g/kg` of commercial glucose gel, same alertness requirement | 2.8P |
| Albuterol | `2.5 mg` by nebulizer, may repeat every `5 min`, **maximum 3 doses** | 2.5 Asthma/COPD |

> **Trap:** Albuterol is on the EMT line only where the agency is approved. The protocol itself says "Agency must be approved by medical director and OEMS."

## The June 24, 2024 waiver

OEMS granted relief from `N.J.A.C. 8:40-7.1(b)6 and 13i` and `8:40A-10.1(b)6 and 13i` so that an approved BLS ambulance service may add four things: **albuterol sulfate** by MDI or nebulizer for wheezing, **CPAP** for shortness of breath secondary to pulmonary edema, **PEEP valves** for any patient requiring BVM ventilation, and **glucometers** for altered mental status suggesting a diabetic emergency.

Approval is per agency, not per EMT. The service submits a cover letter, an education program with curriculum and cognitive exam, written clinical protocols, and policies covering storage, quality assurance and a CLIA waiver, to ems@doh.nj.gov. Source: https://www.nj.gov/health/ems/documents/Expanded_Scope_Application_Instructions.pdf

Naloxone and aspirin appear under the EMT heading in the 2025 protocols but are not written into the `8:40A-10.1(b)` list; treat the protocol plus your agency's standing orders as the operative authority and confirm locally.

> **On shift:** Before your first tour, ask one question: which of the four expanded-scope items is this agency approved for?
keyPoints: Baseline NJ EMT drug authority under 8:40A-10.1(b) is oxygen plus assisting with the patient's own MDI, SL nitroglycerin, and epi auto-injector.
Aspirin 324 mg chewable and adult epinephrine auto-injector 0.3 mg IM are EMT steps in the 2025 protocols.
Naloxone for an EMT is 4 mg nasal spray in one nostril, or 1 mg per nostril by atomizer to a max of 4 mg.
Albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized, max 3 doses, requires agency approval by the medical director and OEMS.
The June 24, 2024 waiver adds albuterol, CPAP, PEEP valves and glucometers per approved agency.

checks.q: A 58-year-old with chest pain took one 81 mg aspirin before you arrived. What does NJ protocol 3.0 direct?
choices: Give nothing further
Give another 81 mg
Give the remaining 243 mg to total 324 mg
Give a full 324 mg on top of the 81 mg
checks.why: The protocol states the total dose taken should be 324 mg, so a patient who took 81 mg receives the remaining 243 mg. Repeating a full 324 mg over-doses; giving nothing under-doses.

checks.q: Which four items did the June 24, 2024 OEMS waiver add to the EMT scope for approved BLS services?
choices: Albuterol, CPAP, PEEP valves, glucometers
Naloxone, aspirin, oral glucose, oxygen
Epinephrine 1:1000 draw-up, IV access, glucometers, CPAP
Nitroglycerin, albuterol, dextrose, PEEP valves
checks.why: The waiver names exactly albuterol sulfate, CPAP, PEEP valves and glucometers. It does not add any drawn-up drug or vascular access, which remain ALS.

checks.q: Under the NJ adult anaphylaxis protocol, what is the EMT epinephrine auto-injector dose and route?
choices: 0.15 mg IM deltoid
0.3 mg IM anterolateral thigh
0.5 mg subcutaneous
1 mg IM anterolateral thigh
checks.why: Protocol 2.2 specifies the adult auto-injector at 0.3 mg IM with the anterolateral thigh as the preferred site; 0.15 mg is the pediatric device. Repeat dosing requires medical command.

lessons.title: Oxygen, PEEP and CPAP under NJ protocol
lessons.body:
New Jersey does not want you flooding people with oxygen. Across the 2025 protocols the target is expressed as a number, not a device: keep `SpO2` at or above `94%`, and `90%` is accepted in COPD. In acute coronary syndrome the instruction is narrower still: give oxygen **only** to patients with dyspnea, hypoxia below `94%`, or signs of heart failure. In stroke the window is `94% to 99%`.

The mechanism is the reason. Supplemental oxygen above what tissue needs does not help a vessel that is blocked, and in ischemic tissue high oxygen tension causes vasoconstriction and free-radical injury. Oxygen is a drug with a target range.

> **Key:** In NJ protocols oxygen is ordered by saturation target, not by liters or mask type.

## PEEP valves

Positive end-expiratory pressure keeps a little back-pressure in the airway at the end of each breath so alveoli do not collapse flat. The June 24, 2024 waiver authorizes **PEEP valves for all patients requiring bag valve mask ventilation** at approved agencies. It is a small attachment on the BVM exhalation port, and it is expanded scope, so it needs agency approval.

## CPAP: the one BLS ventilation adjunct

Protocol `5.3` opens with a sentence worth memorizing: **"CPAP is the only approved adjunct for BLS."**

Indications, all together: a **spontaneously breathing** patient in moderate to severe respiratory distress from congestive heart failure or pulmonary edema, asthma or COPD, pneumonia, submersion injury, or undifferentiated respiratory distress, **plus** oxygen saturation under `94%`, retractions or accessory muscle use, and an adult respiratory rate over `25`.

Contraindications, eight of them:

1. Cardiac or respiratory arrest, or apnea
2. Unable to maintain their own airway
3. Vomiting or active GI bleed
4. Respiratory distress secondary to trauma
5. Suspicion of pneumothorax
6. Agitated or combative and unable to tolerate the mask
7. Facial trauma or an impossible face seal
8. Hypotension with systolic BP under `100 mmHg`

Procedure: explain it and coach the patient through the claustrophobia, sit them upright, apply pulse oximetry, size and assemble the mask, seat it with straps to a minimal leak, then **adjust pressure to `5-10 cm H2O`** to effect. Monitor vitals and pulse oximetry serially. If they improve, keep CPAP for the whole transport and tell the receiving hospital to expect a CPAP patient. **If they deteriorate, take CPAP off and ventilate with a BVM.** Document the time, the provider and the serial oximetry readings.

The asthma and COPD protocol `2.5` adds a specific EMT step: if distress is worsening or severe, provide CPAP with a PEEP of `5 mmHg`.

> **Trap:** Hypotension is a hard stop. CPAP raises intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return and drops preload, so a systolic under `100` gets worse, not better.
keyPoints: NJ protocols target SpO2 at or above 94%, 90% in COPD, 94-99% in stroke, and oxygen only if indicated in ACS.
CPAP is the only approved ventilation adjunct for BLS in New Jersey.
CPAP indications require a spontaneously breathing patient plus SpO2 under 94%, accessory muscle use, and RR over 25.
Pressure is set to 5-10 cm H2O and titrated to effect; deterioration means remove CPAP and use a BVM.
Systolic BP under 100 mmHg, vomiting, trauma, suspected pneumothorax and apnea are contraindications.

checks.q: NJ protocol 5.3 sets what pressure range for CPAP?
choices: 2-4 cm H2O
5-10 cm H2O
10-15 cm H2O
15-20 cm H2O
checks.why: The procedure step reads adjust pressure to 5-10 cm H2O to effect for patient condition. The asthma protocol separately directs starting CPAP with a PEEP of 5.

checks.q: A 70-year-old in pulmonary edema has RR 30, SpO2 88%, BP 86/50. What does NJ protocol allow?
choices: Apply CPAP at 10 cm H2O
Apply CPAP at 5 cm H2O only
Withhold CPAP; systolic under 100 mmHg is a contraindication
Apply CPAP after a fluid bolus
checks.why: Hypotension with SBP under 100 mmHg is listed as a CPAP contraindication because the positive pressure reduces venous return. EMTs also cannot give fluid boluses.

checks.q: In the NJ acute coronary syndrome protocol, when does an EMT give oxygen?
choices: To every chest pain patient at 15 L/min
Only for dyspnea, SpO2 under 94%, or signs of heart failure
Only if the patient requests it
Only after aspirin is given
checks.why: Protocol 3.0 restricts oxygen to patients with dyspnea, hypoxia below 94%, or heart failure signs, titrated to keep saturation at 94% or above. Routine high-flow oxygen is not protocol.

lessons.title: Refusal, capacity and consent in New Jersey
lessons.body:
A competent adult may refuse anything, including care that will save their life. The whole problem is deciding whether the adult in front of you is competent right now, and New Jersey answers that in pieces spread across the protocols rather than in one refusal chapter.

## What the protocols actually say

First, a patient exists earlier than you think. The 2025 protocols define patient contact as beginning when a crew member makes **physical or verbal contact**, and impose an affirmative duty to make every reasonable effort to access potential patients and to document efforts fully when no patient is found.

Second, the behavioral emergencies protocol draws the hard line: **a patient who is a danger to self or others may not refuse care.** If such a patient refuses and needs medical care, contact police and, when available, the local mental health crisis agency.

Third, if the patient is not an immediate threat and refuses transport, the protocol tells you to encourage a mental health evaluation, avoid leaving them alone if possible, and help contact responsible family or friends. The restraint procedure adds that you obtain a refusal of care for patients refusing transport.

Source: NJ EMS Clinical Practice Protocols and Guidelines v1, 8/21/2025.

> **Key:** Capacity is task-specific and present-tense. The question is not "is this person competent" but "can this person, right now, understand this problem, this risk, and this alternative?"

## Building a defensible refusal

There is no single statewide NJ refusal form; agencies use their own, so the content is what protects you. Establish and document that the patient is alert and oriented, that you explained the specific risks in plain language including that they could die, that you offered transport more than once, that you offered to return if they change their mind, and that they demonstrated understanding by saying it back. Vitals, a glucose reading when indicated, and mental status belong in the narrative. If a paramedic is on scene, the transfer-of-care rule matters: care goes to a clinician at the same or higher level unless the condition can be safely managed at the lower level.

## Intoxication and altered mentation

Alcohol, drugs, hypoglycemia, hypoxia, a head strike and hypoperfusion all impair the machinery capacity runs on. A patient who cannot recall the event, cannot state the risk, or has abnormal vitals is telling you something. Correct what you can correct first: check glucose if your agency carries glucometers, give oxygen to target, and re-assess. Naloxone specifically creates this trap, and the protocol answers it: **patients given naloxone should be transported to the emergency department for further evaluation.**

## Minors

Protocol `8.3` defines a minor as anyone who has not reached their eighteenth birthday, and treats minors under **implied consent** when a parent or authorized representative is unavailable. Except in life-threatening emergencies, try to reach the parent or guardian.

A parent or legal guardian may refuse care for a minor, and so may another adult family member or authorized representative with custody when the guardian is not reasonably available. A **telephonic refusal is acceptable** if you explain the consequences and document carefully.

A minor generally may not refuse care. When one tries, the protocol says enlist police, including asking them to place the minor in protective custody; restrain only as a last resort. The exceptions are narrow: a **minor parent** may consent or refuse for their own child if they have capacity; **minors of any age** may consent to treatment associated with rape, incest or sexual abuse; and an **emancipated minor** may consent or refuse, but bears the burden of proving emancipation.

> **On the exam:** Danger to self or others removes the right to refuse. That single sentence answers most NREMT and NJ refusal questions.
keyPoints: NJ protocols say a patient who is a danger to self or others may not refuse care; involve police and the mental health crisis agency.
Patient contact begins at physical or verbal contact, and there is an affirmative duty to locate and document.
Capacity is present-tense and task-specific; correct hypoglycemia and hypoxia before judging it.
Patients given naloxone should be transported for further evaluation.
Minors are under 18; implied consent applies when a guardian is unavailable, and a telephonic parental refusal is acceptable if documented.

checks.q: A patient with a plan to harm himself refuses transport. Under the NJ behavioral emergencies protocol, what is true?
choices: He may refuse if alert and oriented
He may not refuse; contact police and the mental health crisis agency
He may refuse only after speaking with medical command
He may refuse if a family member signs
checks.why: The protocol states a patient who is a danger to self or others may not refuse care, and directs contacting police and, if available, the local mental health crisis agency.

checks.q: A 15-year-old with a wrist injury refuses transport; her mother is at work and reached by phone. What does protocol 8.3 permit?
choices: The minor's own refusal is sufficient
A telephonic refusal by the parent is acceptable if consequences are explained and documented
Only an in-person written parental refusal counts
Police must place her in protective custody
checks.why: Protocol 8.3 expressly allows EMS to accept a telephonic refusal of care after explaining consequences, with careful documentation. The minor herself generally may not refuse.

checks.q: An unresponsive opioid overdose patient wakes after nasal naloxone and wants to stay home. What does the NJ protocol say?
choices: Document a refusal and clear
Patients given naloxone should be transported to the ED for further evaluation
Give a second dose and then clear
Leave the patient with a family member and no transport
checks.why: The altered mental status protocol states patients given naloxone should be transported to the emergency department for further evaluation, because naloxone's duration can be shorter than the opioid's.

lessons.title: DNR, POLST and advance directives in NJ
lessons.body:
The default is resuscitation. Protocol `8.4` and the resuscitation protocol `8.7` say that unless a valid order says otherwise, you work the arrest. The exception is a document, and New Jersey recognizes two kinds.

## The four-step sequence in protocol 8.4

1. A conscious, alert patient's wishes are followed under standard consent procedures. The paper never overrides a talking patient.
2. For a patient who cannot consent, determine whether a valid **Out-of-Hospital DNR** or **POLST** is present.
3. If neither is present, begin standard treatment.
4. If one is present and valid for the clinical state, follow the orders as written, including not beginning or terminating resuscitation.

If you find a different kind of advance directive instead, a living will, a health care proxy, a hospital DNR order, or hospice status, the protocol says **contact medical command early** for direction. A photocopy of an original POLST or Out-of-Hospital DNR is valid.

> **Key:** A DNR answers one question: pulseless, not breathing, unresponsive. POLST answers what to do in the far more common situation where the patient still has a pulse.

## POLST, the part that is easy to get wrong

**POLST** stands for Practitioner Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment. It is a portable **medical order**, not a preference statement. The NJ POLST Act is at `N.J.S.A. 26:2H-129 et seq.`; the Advance Directives for Health Care Act is `N.J.S.A. 26:2H-53 et seq.`

Validity requires a physician or APN signature **and** the signature of the patient or surrogate. Your job, per the protocol: review it for completeness, review the orders before starting treatment, clarify with the patient if they have capacity or with the surrogate, notify medical command, and bring the form with the patient, attaching a copy to your report.

The boxes you will actually read:

- **Section B** sets the treatment level: Full Treatment, Limited Treatment, or comfort-focused care. Limited Treatment paired with "transfer to hospital only if comfort needs cannot be met in current location" means you transport for comfort and symptom relief.
- **Section D** is the critical-patient section. Pulseless or apneic, it says attempt resuscitation or DNAR. With a pulse and in respiratory distress, it says whether to intubate; if do-not-intubate, you still provide other relief such as oxygen, medications and manual relief of airway obstruction.
- **Section E** names the surrogate decision maker, who may void or modify the form.
- **Section F** carries the signatures and license number.

> **Trap:** A blank box is not a refusal. The protocol states that if a box is left blank, the assumption is that treatment **will** be provided for that category.

## The Out-of-Hospital DNR

New Jersey's Out-of-Hospital DNR protocol dates to 1997 and uses a standardized form signed by the patient or surrogate and the attending physician or APN, with an optional MSNJ-approved DNR bracelet accepted as evidence of a valid order. Legible photocopies are acceptable. It may be revoked at any time by destroying the form and bracelet, by the patient saying out loud they intend to revoke, or by the attending physician or at the surrogate's direction. Source: NJ-ACEP/MSNJ New Jersey Out-of-Hospital DNR guidelines, August 2003, https://www.njha.com/media/33214/DNRGuidelines.pdf

Because that booklet is old, treat protocol `8.4` from 8/21/2025 as the operative EMS instruction and use the booklet only for form and bracelet detail.

> **On shift:** If you cannot verify validity in the seconds you have, start resuscitation and call medical command. Starting is reversible; not starting is not.
keyPoints: Default is full resuscitation unless a valid Out-of-Hospital DNR or POLST is present and applies.
A conscious alert patient's stated wishes govern regardless of the paperwork.
POLST is a medical order requiring a physician or APN signature plus patient or surrogate signature; copies are valid.
A blank POLST box means treatment will be provided for that category.
Living wills, proxies, hospital DNRs and hospice status are not field DNRs; contact medical command early.

checks.q: You find a POLST with Section D completed but the artificial nutrition box blank. How do you treat that blank box?
choices: As a refusal of that treatment
As invalidating the entire form
As meaning treatment will be provided for that category
As requiring the surrogate to complete it before any care
checks.why: Protocol 8.4 states that if a box is left blank, the assumption is that treatment will be provided for that category. A blank never means refusal, and it does not void the form.

checks.q: A family presents a living will for an unresponsive patient in cardiac arrest. What does the NJ protocol direct?
choices: Honor it as a DNR
Begin standard treatment and contact medical command early for direction
Refuse to transport
Have the family sign a refusal
checks.why: A living will is an advance directive, not a portable medical order. Protocol 8.4 directs contacting medical command early when other forms of advance directive are present.

checks.q: Which statement about the NJ Out-of-Hospital DNR is correct?
choices: Only the original form is valid, never a copy
An approved DNR bracelet is accepted as evidence of a valid order
It can only be revoked in writing
It applies to a patient who has a pulse and is breathing
checks.why: The MSNJ-approved bracelet is accepted as valid evidence, legible photocopies are acceptable, and revocation may be oral. A DNR applies only to cardiac and respiratory arrest.

lessons.title: Where the patient goes: trauma, stroke and STEMI in South Jersey
lessons.body:
The general rule in protocol `1.0` is the closest appropriate hospital, with the destination chosen by the highest-level clinician on scene. Then it adds the exception that runs your career: **regionalized systems of care for STEMI, stroke and trauma may require transport past a closer hospital.**

## Trauma

Protocol `8.2` adopts the **National Guideline for the Field Triage of Injured Patients**, with RED criteria for high risk of serious injury and YELLOW criteria for moderate risk. Protocol `1.0` adds the operational numbers: patients meeting trauma criteria go expeditiously to a trauma center, **on-scene time under `10 minutes` post-extrication**, and on-scene care limited to the primary assessment, rapid trauma assessment and life-saving interventions.

New Jersey designates **ten** trauma centers. Three are Level I: **Cooper University Hospital** in Camden, **University Hospital** in Newark, and **Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital** in New Brunswick. The Level II centers are AtlantiCare Regional Medical Center City Campus in Atlantic City, Hackensack University Medical Center, Jersey City Medical Center, Capital Health Regional Medical Center in Trenton, Jersey Shore University Medical Center in Neptune, Morristown Medical Center, and St. Joseph's University Medical Center in Paterson. Source: NJ DOH OEMS trauma center list, https://www.nj.gov/health/ems/documents/NJ%20Trauma%20Centers.pdf

For South Jersey that means exactly two designated options: **Cooper, the only Level I south of Trenton**, and AtlantiCare City Campus at Level II. Cooper is the regional trauma center for Atlantic, Burlington, Camden, Cape May, Cumberland, Gloucester, Mercer, Ocean and Salem counties.

> **Key:** In South Jersey, "trauma center" usually means Cooper. Everything else is a community ED that will package and move the patient again.

## Stroke

Protocol `2.23` gives the EMT four jobs. Perform a stroke assessment using **B.E. F.A.S.T.** If positive, run the **R.A.C.E.** scale for large vessel occlusion; for a **R.A.C.E. score above `5`**, consider transporting directly to a Comprehensive Stroke Center based on local protocol. Establish stroke alert criteria and notify the hospital of "Stroke Alert and Time Last Known Well." Then treat: oxygen to `94-99%`, glucose check if your agency is approved for glucometry, head of stretcher to `30 degrees` unless spinal motion restriction is needed, minimize scene time, and **do not delay for ALS intercept**. Try to get a phone number for family or a witness.

New Jersey designates stroke centers in four tiers: Acute Stroke Ready Hospital, Primary, Thrombectomy-Capable, and Comprehensive. **Cooper University Hospital is a Comprehensive Stroke Center.** The Department of Health publishes the county-by-county list; the specific tier of every other South Jersey hospital changes with recertification, so check the current list rather than memorizing it. Source: https://www.nj.gov/health/healthcarequality/documents/Website_Designated_Stroke_Centers_July2026a.pdf

## STEMI

Protocol `3.0` gives EMTs one destination rule, and it is conditional on ALS: call for ALS intercept, and **if ALS is unavailable, transport to an interventional cardiac catheterization capable hospital if greater than 10 minutes.** The 12-lead and the STEMI confirmation are paramedic steps, so at BLS your contribution is aspirin, a saturation-targeted oxygen decision, assisting the patient's own nitroglycerin, early notification, and not sitting on scene.

> **On the exam:** Bypassing a closer hospital is correct only when a regionalized system, trauma, stroke or STEMI, says so. Otherwise closest appropriate wins.
keyPoints: Default destination is the closest appropriate hospital; STEMI, stroke and trauma systems are the exception.
Trauma scene time should be under 10 minutes post-extrication, with care limited to primary and rapid trauma assessment.
NJ has 10 designated trauma centers; Cooper in Camden is the only Level I in South Jersey.
Stroke: B.E. F.A.S.T. then R.A.C.E.; a R.A.C.E. score above 5 prompts considering a Comprehensive Stroke Center.
If ALS is unavailable, a suspected STEMI goes to a cath-capable hospital when transport exceeds 10 minutes.

choices: AtlantiCare Regional Medical Center City Campus
Cooper University Hospital, Camden
Virtua Voorhees
Jersey Shore University Medical Center
checks.why: The NJ OEMS list shows three Level I centers: Cooper, University Hospital Newark, and RWJUH New Brunswick. AtlantiCare City Campus is Level II and Jersey Shore is Level II in Monmouth County.

choices: Greater than 2
Greater than 5
Greater than 8
Any positive B.E. F.A.S.T.
checks.why: The protocol flags a R.A.C.E. score above 5 as the trigger to consider a Comprehensive Stroke Center, based on local protocol. A positive B.E. F.A.S.T. alone prompts the R.A.C.E. assessment.

choices: Under 5 minutes from arrival
Under 10 minutes post-extrication
Under 20 minutes total
No specific limit
checks.why: Protocol 1.0 directs minimizing on-scene time to less than 10 minutes post-extrication and limiting on-scene care to primary assessment, rapid trauma assessment and life-saving interventions.

lessons.title: Mandatory reporting and legal duties in NJ
lessons.body:
New Jersey turns some of what you see into something you are legally required to say. Two reporting duties reach every EMT, and one behavioral-health pathway shapes where psychiatric patients end up.

## Child abuse: everyone reports

Under `N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.10`, **any person** with reasonable cause to believe a child has been subjected to abuse or neglect must report it immediately. New Jersey has no professional-only list; everyone is a mandated reporter.

The 2025 protocols, section `8.0`, put operational detail on it. Report to the **State Central Registry** at **1-877-NJ-ABUSE**; if the child is in immediate danger, call law enforcement as well. You do not need proof, and the call can be anonymous.

The sentence that matters most on shift: **the report should be made by the provider directly. Relying on another healthcare provider or on law enforcement to make the report is inappropriate.** Handing off at triage does not discharge your duty.

Good-faith reporters are immune from criminal and civil liability. Knowingly failing to report is a disorderly persons offense punishable by a fine up to `$1,000`, up to six months imprisonment, or both.

The protocol also directs taking suspected child abuse patients to a hospital with appropriate resources unless they are unstable and need the closest facility, and warns you not to confront suspected perpetrators.

> **Key:** Report directly, from the field or as soon as practical, and document that you did.

## Vulnerable adults

New Jersey's Adult Protective Services law, `N.J.S.A. 52:27D-406 to 426`, was amended to require health care professionals, law enforcement officers, firefighters, paramedics and **emergency medical technicians** with reasonable cause to believe a vulnerable adult is being abused, neglected or exploited to report it to the **county Adult Protective Services** office. Abuse there means willful infliction of physical pain, injury or mental anguish, unreasonable confinement, or willful deprivation of services needed to maintain physical and mental health.

## Involuntary commitment screening

When a patient is dangerous to self, others or property because of mental illness, the destination is often a designated **screening service**. Under `N.J.S.A. 30:4-27.1 et seq.`, the Commissioner of Human Services designates screening services by county or region. A mental health screener who finds reasonable cause to believe the person needs involuntary commitment executes a **screening certificate**, which lets a facility detain the person without a court order for **no more than `72` hours**, during which commitment proceedings must be started. Source: N.J.S.A. 30:4-27.5.

You do not certify anyone. What you do is recognize the pathway, use police assistance for a patient who cannot refuse because they are a danger, and hand off a clean, behavioral description: what they said, what they did, what they have access to.

## Restraints

Protocol `6.5` sets limits. Restraints must not cause undue discomfort, harm or pain. **Hard restraints such as handcuffs are prohibited unless the law enforcement officer who applied them personally accompanies the patient.** Patients are not transported in restraints unless a physician or court authorized it or the protocol's criteria are met, and the chart must record the reason, the type, the time applied, circulation checks and any resulting injury. The behavioral protocol adds an absolute: **at no time shall a patient be placed in the prone position.**

> **Trap:** Struggling against restraints can cause hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis and cardiac arrest. A quiet restrained patient is not automatically a stable one; keep reassessing.

## Safe Haven

New Jersey's Safe Haven Infant Protection Act lets a parent anonymously surrender a newborn at a police station, fire station, hospital emergency department or ambulance squad. Protocol `8.8` directs calling the Department of Children and Families Safe Haven hotline at **1-877-839-2339** no later than the first business day after the baby is received, and protecting the parent's anonymity.
keyPoints: In NJ every person is a mandated child abuse reporter under N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.10; call 1-877-NJ-ABUSE.
The EMS provider must report directly; delegating to hospital staff or police is inappropriate.
Failing to report knowingly is a disorderly persons offense, up to $1,000 fine and six months jail.
EMTs must report suspected abuse of vulnerable adults to county Adult Protective Services.
A screening certificate allows detention up to 72 hours; handcuffs require the applying officer to ride along; never transport prone.

The officer who applied the handcuffs must personally accompany the patient
Handcuffs may be used if documented
Transport prone with the handcuffs behind the back

48 hours
