lessons.title: The New Jersey PA practice act
lessons.body:
You are pointed at physician assistant school, so it is worth knowing now what the license you are chasing actually permits in this state. New Jersey's rules sit in two places: the **Physician Assistant Licensing Act**, `N.J.S.A. 45:9-27.10 et seq.` (P.L. 1991, c. 378), and the Board of Medical Examiners regulations at `N.J.A.C. 13:35-2B`.

## Getting licensed

`N.J.A.C. 13:35-2B.5` requires that an applicant be at least `18`, be of good moral character, graduate from a PA education program accredited by the **Accreditation Review Commission on Education for the Physician Assistant (ARC-PA)**, and pass the examination given by the **National Commission on Certification of Physician Assistants (NCCPA)**, which is the PANCE. Holders of a substantially equivalent license in another state may satisfy these without repeating each step.

## Keeping it

Licenses renew **biennially** under `13:35-2B.7`. `13:35-2B.8` sets **50 continuing education credit hours per biennial period**, in Category I courses approved by the AMA, AAPA, AAFP, AOA or ACCME. At least one credit must cover prescription opioid drugs, responsible prescribing, alternatives for pain, and the risks and signs of opioid abuse, addiction and diversion. PAs providing perinatal care must also complete one credit of evidence-based explicit and implicit bias training. Up to `15` credits earned in the last six months of a period may carry into the next one.

> **Key:** Compare the cycles. Your EMT card is 48 hours over 36 months. A NJ PA license is 50 hours every 24 months, with named required topics.

## Supervision, not independent practice

New Jersey is a supervision state, not a full-practice-authority state. A PA practices under the supervision of a physician at all times while working in an official capacity. Supervision is **continuous but does not require physical presence**, provided the physician and PA maintain contact electronically or by other means. `N.J.A.C. 13:35-2B.10` caps the ratio at **four PAs per supervising physician** unless the Board alters it on application.

The mechanism is a written **delegation agreement**, executed separately with each supervising physician, signed and dated **annually**, updated when the role changes, kept on file at the practice site and filed with the Physician Assistant Advisory Committee. The agreement states the PA's role, the practice locations, and whether the physician requires personal chart review and countersignature of services performed.

A PA may provide any medical service delegated by the supervising physician, so long as the service is within the PA's skills, is a component of the physician's own scope, and is provided under supervision. That is the whole scope test in one sentence, and it is why two NJ PAs in different specialties can have very different day-to-day scopes.

## Prescribing

A PA may order, prescribe, dispense and administer medications and devices to the extent delegated. Controlled dangerous substances require more: the supervising physician must authorize Schedule II, III, IV or V prescribing, the PA must be registered with the DEA, and the PA prints their DEA number on the order. The statute distinguishes continuing or reissuing a physician's existing CDS order, adjusting a dose with prior consultation, and initiating a new CDS order with prior consultation.

> **On shift:** COVID-era executive orders had suspended the supervision and delegation-agreement requirements. Executive Order 415 of January 16, 2026 terminated those waivers, and after an extension under Executive Order 13 they ended at 5:00 PM on April 2, 2026. NJ PAs are again fully subject to the statutory supervision and delegation-agreement rules, so anything you read from 2020 to 2025 describing waived supervision is out of date.
keyPoints: NJ PA licensure requires an ARC-PA accredited program and passing the NCCPA exam, under N.J.A.C. 13:35-2B.5.
Licenses renew biennially with 50 Category I CE credits, including one opioid-prescribing credit.
New Jersey requires physician supervision, continuous but not necessarily in person, capped at four PAs per physician.
A written delegation agreement is signed annually with each supervising physician and kept on file.
CDS prescribing requires physician authorization, DEA registration, and prior consultation to initiate.

checks.q: How many PAs may one New Jersey physician supervise under N.J.A.C. 13:35-2B.10 absent Board action?
choices: Two
Three
Four
Unlimited
checks.why: The rule caps supervision at four physician assistants per supervising physician, though the Board may alter the ratio upon application.

checks.q: What continuing education does a NJ PA need per biennial renewal period?
choices: 25 Category I credits
50 Category I credits including one opioid-prescribing credit
100 credits of any type
48 credits over 36 months
checks.why: N.J.A.C. 13:35-2B.8 requires 50 Category I credit hours biennially with at least one credit on prescription opioid drugs. The 48-over-36-months figure is the EMT rule, not the PA rule.

checks.q: Which statement best describes the NJ PA scope-of-practice test?
choices: A PA may perform any service listed in a state formulary
A PA may perform any service delegated by the supervising physician that is within the PA's skills and a component of the physician's scope
A PA has independent practice authority after 2,000 hours
A PA may only perform services personally observed by the physician
checks.why: The statute defines a physician-delegated scope: the service must be delegated, within the PA's skills, part of the supervising physician's scope, and provided under supervision. Supervision does not require physical presence.

cards.front: Which New Jersey agency issues the certification card that lets you work as an EMT here?
cards.back: The NJ Office of Emergency Medical Services (OEMS), within the NJ Department of Health. NREMT writes and scores the exam; OEMS issues and disciplines the certification.

cards.front: Which chapter of the NJ Administrative Code governs EMT-Basic training and certification?
cards.back: N.J.A.C. 8:40A, "Emergency Medical Technicians-Basics: Training and Certification."

cards.front: What three requirements does N.J.A.C. 8:40A-7.2 set for initial EMT-Basic certification?
cards.back: Age 18; current CPR certification; completion of an approved EMT-Basic program including a 10-hour clinical experience plus a passing NREMT-Basic certification exam score (or reciprocity).

cards.front: How long is a NJ EMT-Basic certification valid?
cards.back: Not less than 36 and not more than 42 months. Recertifications are valid through the card's expiration date but never more than 36 months from issue.

cards.front: How many CEU hours does NJ recertification require, and split how?
cards.back: 48 hours: 24 core plus 24 elective, accrued in the 36 months immediately before recertification.

cards.front: Do unused NJ EMT continuing education credits carry into the next cycle?
cards.back: No. At the start of each recertification period the balance resets to zero core and zero elective credits.

cards.front: What must someone do if their NJ EMT certification has expired?
cards.back: Complete an approved Core 13 program and pass the NREMT-Basic certification examination again, under N.J.A.C. 8:40A-7.6.

cards.front: Which out-of-state EMT certifications get automatic status in NJ under 8:40A-7.3?
cards.back: NREMT, New York, and Atlantic EMS Council member states: Delaware, DC, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Virginia, West Virginia. A NJ card still requires an application and Core 13.

cards.front: What limits apply to a 17-year-old with provisional NJ EMT status?
cards.back: They work only in the physical presence and under direct supervision of a certified EMT, and cannot count toward minimum personnel on an ambulance.

cards.front: What is the name and version date of New Jersey's current statewide EMS protocol document?
cards.back: New Jersey EMS Clinical Practice Protocols and Guidelines, version 1, dated 8/21/2025, published by NJ DOH OEMS.

cards.front: In a NJ protocol number like 2.8P, what does the P mean?
cards.back: It is the pediatric version of that protocol. An A suffix means adult. No suffix means it applies to both.

cards.front: In what order do the treatment headings appear inside a NJ protocol?
cards.back: EMT first, then Paramedic and MICN, then Communication Failure where it exists.

cards.front: Can a NJ agency medical director expand an EMT's scope of practice?
cards.back: No. The protocols state a medical director may restrict, but not expand, the scope of practice at each provider level.

cards.front: What does it mean that NJ standing orders are cumulative?
cards.back: A higher credential's standing orders include everything authorized at lower levels, and any clinician may switch between or combine protocols as the patient's condition changes.

cards.front: When must a NJ EMS clinician contact on-line medical command?
cards.back: When treatment beyond standing orders is needed or physician input is required. Medical command may not authorize a procedure outside your defined scope.

cards.front: Which nine sections organize the NJ protocol document?
cards.back: 1 General Patient Care, 2 Medical, 3 Cardiac, 4 Trauma, 5 Airway, 6 Medical Procedures, 7 Prerequisite, 8 Medical Policies, 9 Hazmat and MCI.

cards.front: What three prescribed medications does N.J.A.C. 8:40A-10.1(b)13 let an EMT assist a patient in taking?
cards.back: The patient's own prescribed metered dose inhaler, sublingual nitroglycerin, and epinephrine auto-injector.

cards.front: What aspirin dose does NJ protocol 3.0 direct an EMT to give in suspected ACS?
cards.back: 324 mg PO chewable. If the patient already took 81 mg, give the remaining 243 mg so the total is 324 mg.

cards.front: Under NJ protocol 3.0, what are the limits on assisting with nitroglycerin?
cards.back: Facilitate the patient's own nitroglycerin every 3 to 5 minutes while symptoms persist and systolic BP stays at or above 100 mmHg, to a total of 3 doses.

cards.front: What is the NJ EMT adult epinephrine auto-injector dose and preferred site for anaphylaxis?
cards.back: 0.3 mg IM, anterolateral thigh preferred. Repeat dosing requires contacting medical command.

cards.front: What is the pediatric epinephrine auto-injector strength named in NJ protocol 2.2P?
cards.back: The age and weight appropriate 0.15 mg auto-injector.

cards.front: What are the two EMT naloxone formulations and doses in NJ protocol 2.3A?
cards.back: Nasal spray 4 mg into one nostril, or 1 mg (1 mL) per nostril by atomizer to a maximum of 4 mg. The initial dose may be repeated after 5 minutes.

cards.front: What oral glucose dose does NJ protocol give for an adult hypoglycemic patient?
cards.back: 1 to 2 tubes of commercially prepared glucose gel. The patient must be alert enough to swallow and protect their airway.

cards.front: What is the pediatric oral glucose dose in NJ protocol 2.8P?
cards.back: 0.5 g/kg of commercially prepared glucose gel, with the same requirement that the child can swallow and protect the airway.

cards.front: What albuterol dose and maximum does the NJ asthma/COPD protocol give an EMT?
cards.back: 2.5 mg by nebulizer, may repeat every 5 minutes, maximum 3 doses, and only where the agency is approved by its medical director and OEMS.

cards.front: What four items did the June 24, 2024 OEMS waiver add to NJ EMT scope?
cards.back: Albuterol sulfate by MDI or nebulizer, CPAP, PEEP valves, and glucometers, for BLS ambulance services approved through OEMS.

cards.front: Is expanded-scope approval in NJ granted to the individual EMT or the agency?
cards.back: The agency. A BLS ambulance service applies to OEMS with education, protocols and policies; individual EMTs then work under that approval.

cards.front: What SpO2 target do the NJ protocols use generally, and what is accepted in COPD?
cards.back: At or above 94%; 90% is accepted in COPD. In stroke the target window is 94 to 99%.

cards.front: When does NJ protocol 3.0 permit oxygen in acute coronary syndrome?
cards.back: Only for dyspnea, hypoxia with SpO2 under 94%, or signs of heart failure, titrated to keep saturation at 94% or above.

cards.front: What single sentence opens NJ protocol 5.3 about BLS ventilation adjuncts?
cards.back: "CPAP is the only approved adjunct for BLS."

cards.front: What three objective findings accompany the NJ CPAP indications?
cards.back: Oxygen saturation under 94%, retractions or accessory muscle use, and an adult respiratory rate over 25, in a spontaneously breathing patient in moderate to severe distress.

cards.front: List the NJ CPAP contraindications.
cards.back: Arrest or apnea, inability to maintain an airway, vomiting or active GI bleed, distress from trauma, suspected pneumothorax, agitation preventing mask tolerance, facial trauma or no seal, and SBP under 100 mmHg.

cards.front: What pressure range does NJ protocol 5.3 set for CPAP?
cards.back: 5 to 10 cm H2O, adjusted to effect for the patient's condition.

cards.front: What does NJ protocol direct if a patient deteriorates on CPAP?
cards.back: Discontinue CPAP and assist respirations with a bag valve mask.

cards.front: What starting PEEP does the NJ asthma/COPD protocol name for worsening or severe distress?
cards.back: CPAP with a PEEP of 5 mmHg.

cards.front: Which patients may get a PEEP valve under the 2024 NJ waiver?
cards.back: All patients requiring bag valve mask ventilation, at agencies approved for the expanded scope.

cards.front: When does patient contact begin under the NJ protocols?
cards.back: When a crew member makes physical or verbal contact with a patient. There is an affirmative duty to make every reasonable effort to access potential patients.

cards.front: Can a NJ patient who is a danger to self or others refuse care?
cards.back: No. The behavioral emergencies protocol states such a patient may not refuse; contact police and, if available, the local mental health crisis agency.

cards.front: What disposition does NJ protocol set for a patient who received naloxone?
cards.back: They should be transported to the emergency department for further evaluation.

cards.front: How does NJ protocol 8.3 define a minor?
cards.back: A person who has not yet reached their eighteenth birthday. That legal definition is separate from the clinical terms pediatric patient, child and children.

cards.front: May NJ EMS accept a parent's refusal of care for a minor over the phone?
cards.back: Yes, provided the consequences of refusing are explained and the telephonic refusal is carefully documented.

cards.front: What does NJ protocol direct when a minor tries to refuse care and transport?
cards.back: A minor generally may not refuse. Enlist police, including a request to place the minor in protective custody. Restrain only as a last resort.

cards.front: Name the three special circumstances in which a NJ minor may consent to or refuse care.
cards.back: A minor parent deciding for their own child with capacity; any minor consenting to treatment associated with rape, incest or sexual abuse; and an emancipated minor who can establish emancipation.

cards.front: What is the default resuscitation posture under NJ protocol 8.4?
cards.back: Full resuscitation. Only a valid Out-of-Hospital DNR or POLST that applies to the patient's clinical state changes it.

cards.front: Whose wishes govern when the patient is conscious and alert and a POLST exists?
cards.back: The patient's. Protocol 8.4 says the wishes of conscious, alert patients are followed under standard consent procedures.

cards.front: What does POLST stand for and what kind of document is it?
cards.back: Practitioner Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment: a portable medical order, not a preference statement, that all healthcare professionals must follow.

cards.front: What signatures make a NJ POLST valid?
cards.back: A physician or APN signature plus the signature of the patient or surrogate. A legible copy of the original is valid.

cards.front: How does a DNR differ in scope from a POLST?
cards.back: A DNR applies only when the patient is pulseless, not breathing and unresponsive. A POLST also directs care for a patient who still has a pulse, is breathing, or is responsive.

cards.front: What does a blank box on a NJ POLST mean?
cards.back: The assumption is that treatment will be provided for that category. A blank is never a refusal.

cards.front: What should NJ EMS do when a living will, health care proxy, hospital DNR or hospice status is presented instead of a DNR or POLST?
cards.back: Contact medical command early for further direction.

cards.front: What NJ statutes cover POLST and advance directives?
cards.back: The POLST Act at N.J.S.A. 26:2H-129 et seq., and the New Jersey Advance Directives for Health Care Act at N.J.S.A. 26:2H-53 et seq.

cards.front: What is the default destination rule in NJ protocol 1.0, and who decides?
cards.back: The closest appropriate hospital, with destination and transport mode determined by the EMS clinician with the highest level of training on scene.

cards.front: Which three systems of care justify bypassing a closer NJ hospital?
cards.back: STEMI, stroke and trauma. Regionalized systems of care for those may require transport to a specific facility.

cards.front: What on-scene time does NJ protocol set for trauma patients meeting criteria?
cards.back: Less than 10 minutes post-extrication, with care limited to primary assessment, rapid trauma assessment and life-saving interventions.

cards.front: Name New Jersey's three Level I trauma centers.
cards.back: Cooper University Hospital in Camden, University Hospital in Newark, and Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital in New Brunswick.

cards.front: Which trauma centers serve South Jersey, and at what levels?
cards.back: Cooper University Hospital in Camden at Level I, and AtlantiCare Regional Medical Center City Campus in Atlantic City at Level II.

cards.front: What two stroke scales does NJ protocol 2.23 put in the EMT's hands?
cards.back: B.E. F.A.S.T. for the initial stroke assessment, and the R.A.C.E. scale for large vessel occlusion if B.E. F.A.S.T. is positive.

cards.front: At what R.A.C.E. score does NJ protocol suggest considering a Comprehensive Stroke Center?
cards.back: A score greater than 5, based on local protocol.

cards.front: What does a NJ EMT report to the hospital on a stroke alert?
cards.back: "Stroke Alert and Time Last Known Well." Also try to obtain a phone number for family or a witness to the event.

cards.front: What are the four NJ stroke center designation tiers?
cards.back: Acute Stroke Ready Hospital, Primary Stroke Center, Thrombectomy-Capable Stroke Center, and Comprehensive Stroke Center, designated by NJ DOH.

cards.front: What destination rule does NJ protocol 3.0 give an EMT when no ALS is available for a suspected STEMI?
cards.back: Transport to an interventional cardiac catheterization capable hospital if transport is greater than 10 minutes.

cards.front: Who is a mandated child abuse reporter in New Jersey?
cards.back: Any person. N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.10 requires anyone with reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused or neglected to report immediately.

cards.front: What number does NJ EMS call to report suspected child abuse?
cards.back: The State Central Registry at 1-877-NJ-ABUSE. If the child is in immediate danger, call law enforcement as well.

cards.front: Can a NJ EMT satisfy the child abuse reporting duty by telling the ED staff?
cards.back: No. The protocol says the report should be made by the provider directly; relying on another healthcare provider or law enforcement is inappropriate.

cards.front: What is the penalty in NJ for knowingly failing to report suspected child abuse?
cards.back: It is a disorderly persons offense punishable by a fine up to $1,000, up to six months imprisonment, or both. Good-faith reporters have immunity.

cards.front: To whom must a NJ EMT report suspected abuse of a vulnerable adult?
cards.back: The county Adult Protective Services office, under N.J.S.A. 52:27D-406 to 426, which names EMTs among mandated reporters.

cards.front: How long may a NJ facility hold a person on a screening certificate without a court order?
cards.back: No more than 72 hours from execution of the certificate, during which involuntary commitment proceedings must be initiated (N.J.S.A. 30:4-27.5).

cards.front: When may a patient in handcuffs be transported by NJ EMS?
cards.back: Only when the law enforcement officer who applied the hard restraints personally accompanies the patient. Hard restraints are otherwise prohibited.

cards.front: What positioning is absolutely prohibited for a restrained NJ patient?
cards.back: Prone. The behavioral protocol states at no time shall a patient be placed in the prone position.

cards.front: What is the NJ Safe Haven hotline number and when is it called?
cards.back: 1-877-839-2339, no later than the first business day after a baby is received. NJ's Safe Haven Infant Protection Act protects the surrendering parent's anonymity.

cards.front: Which two authorities govern physician assistant practice in New Jersey?
cards.back: The Physician Assistant Licensing Act, N.J.S.A. 45:9-27.10 et seq., and Board of Medical Examiners rules at N.J.A.C. 13:35-2B.

cards.front: What education and exam does NJ require for PA licensure?
cards.back: Graduation from an ARC-PA accredited PA program and a passing score on the NCCPA examination, plus being at least 18 and of good moral character.

cards.front: How often does a NJ PA license renew, and with how much CE?
cards.back: Biennially, with 50 Category I continuing education credit hours per period.

cards.front: Which CE topics are specifically required of NJ PAs?
cards.back: At least one credit on prescription opioid drugs and responsible prescribing, and for PAs providing perinatal care, one credit of explicit and implicit bias training.

cards.front: Does NJ require a PA's supervising physician to be physically present?
cards.back: No. Supervision must be continuous but does not require physical presence, as long as physician and PA maintain contact electronically or by other means.

cards.front: How many PAs may one NJ physician supervise?
cards.back: Four, under N.J.A.C. 13:35-2B.10, unless the Board alters the ratio on application.

cards.front: What is a NJ PA delegation agreement and how often is it signed?
cards.back: A written agreement executed separately with each supervising physician, signed and dated annually, updated as the role changes, kept at the practice site and filed with the PA Advisory Committee.

cards.front: What is the three-part test for whether a NJ PA may perform a service?
cards.back: It must be delegated by the supervising physician, within the PA's skills, and a component of the supervising physician's own scope of practice, provided under supervision.

cards.front: What extra conditions apply to a NJ PA prescribing controlled dangerous substances?
cards.back: The supervising physician must authorize Schedule II-V prescribing, the PA must register with the DEA and print the DEA number on the order, and initiating a new CDS order requires prior consultation.

cards.front: What happened to the NJ COVID-era waivers of PA supervision requirements?
cards.back: Executive Order 415 of January 16, 2026 terminated them; after an extension under Executive Order 13 they ended at 5:00 PM on April 2, 2026. Statutory supervision and delegation agreements apply again.

quiz.q: Which body issues the certification that legally permits you to practice as an EMT in New Jersey?
choices: The NJ Office of Emergency Medical Services
Your agency's medical director
The NJ Board of Medical Examiners
The National Registry of EMTs
quiz.why: OEMS, inside the NJ Department of Health, issues and disciplines NJ EMT certification. NREMT only administers the exam; the medical director controls agency-level scope; the BME licenses physicians and PAs.

quiz.q: An EMT's NJ card expires in eight months and she has 30 CEU hours logged, 20 of them from 40 months ago. How many of those count toward recertification?
choices: All 30
Only the 10 earned within the last 36 months
20, since core hours never expire
None; all CEUs must be earned in the final year
quiz.why: N.J.A.C. 8:40A-7.5(b) counts only the 48 hours accrued in the 36 months immediately before recertification. Hours older than that window and leftover credits from a prior cycle do not count.

quiz.q: A Pennsylvania-certified EMT wants a New Jersey card. What does N.J.A.C. 8:40A-7.3 require?
choices: Only proof of employment with a NJ agency
Nothing; PA certification is fully interchangeable
A reciprocity application, an approved Core 13 program, a certificate of eligibility, and a passing NREMT assessment exam
A full NJ EMT course from the beginning
quiz.why: Pennsylvania is an Atlantic EMS Council state, so the EMT has status in NJ, but obtaining a NJ card requires the application, Core 13, certificate of eligibility and NREMT assessment exam. It is neither automatic nor a full repeat course.

quiz.q: Your agency medical director announces the agency will not carry CPAP even though the service is approved for it. Is this permissible?
choices: Yes, but only with OEMS written consent
No, OEMS approval overrides the medical director
No, CPAP is mandatory once approved
Yes, a medical director may restrict but not expand scope
quiz.why: The 2025 protocols state medical directors may restrict, but not expand, scope at each provider level. Restricting a permitted skill is within their authority; adding one is not.

quiz.q: You are reading NJ protocol 2.12P. What does the number tell you?
choices: Section 2, medical protocols, pediatric version
Section 2, paramedic-only protocol
Protocol requiring medical command
Section 12, pediatric procedures
quiz.why: The leading digit is the section, medical protocols being section 2, and the P suffix marks the pediatric version. Paramedic steps are marked by heading inside the protocol, not by the number.

quiz.q: Medical command physician orders an EMT to start an IV during a long transport. What is the correct response?
choices: Comply only if the patient is unstable
Decline; medical command may not authorize procedures outside your defined scope
Comply and document the physician's name
Comply; on-line medical command can authorize any order
quiz.why: The protocol preface states medical command may not direct or authorize clinicians to perform procedures outside their defined scope. IV access is not in the NJ EMT scope under any patient condition.

quiz.q: A 62-year-old with crushing chest pain took a single 81 mg aspirin 10 minutes ago. Systolic BP is 138. What does NJ protocol 3.0 direct the EMT to give?
choices: No further aspirin
81 mg more
243 mg more, for a total of 324 mg
324 mg more
quiz.why: The protocol specifies a total taken dose of 324 mg, so a patient who took 81 mg receives the remaining 243 mg. Giving nothing leaves the patient under-dosed; a full 324 mg on top would exceed protocol.

quiz.q: The same patient has his own nitroglycerin. Under NJ protocol, what governs assisting him?
choices: One dose only, then ALS must take over
Only with an on-line medical command order
Every 5 minutes to a total of 5 doses regardless of BP
Every 3 to 5 minutes while symptoms persist, systolic at or above 100 mmHg, maximum 3 doses
quiz.why: Protocol 3.0 sets nitroglycerin assistance at every 3 to 5 minutes while symptoms persist with a systolic at or above 100 mmHg, to a total of 3 doses. Blood pressure is the gate because nitrates drop preload.

quiz.q: Which of these is an EMT-level medication under the NJ 2025 protocols without any expanded-scope approval?
choices: Aspirin 324 mg chewable
Dextrose 10% IV
Albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized
Diphenhydramine 25 mg IM
quiz.why: Aspirin appears under the EMT heading in protocol 3.0. Albuterol requires agency approval by the medical director and OEMS; diphenhydramine and dextrose are paramedic and MICN interventions.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old in anaphylaxis after a bee sting has hives, stridor and a BP of 82/44. Your agency has auto-injectors. What is the correct NJ EMT action?
choices: Diphenhydramine first, epinephrine only if no improvement
Epinephrine auto-injector 0.3 mg IM anterolateral thigh, then transport without delay
Epinephrine 0.15 mg IM deltoid
Wait for ALS before giving epinephrine
quiz.why: Protocol 2.2 has the EMT give the adult 0.3 mg auto-injector in the anterolateral thigh and states DO NOT DELAY TRANSPORT. 0.15 mg is the pediatric device, diphenhydramine is a paramedic drug, and waiting for ALS risks airway loss.

quiz.q: How many doses of naloxone nasal spray may a NJ EMT give an adult under protocol 2.3A using the 4 mg formulation?
choices: Unlimited until the patient wakes
One only
The initial dose, repeatable once after 5 minutes
Up to four sprays back to back
quiz.why: The protocol allows a single 4 mg spray into one nostril with the initial dose repeatable after 5 minutes. The alternate formulation is 1 mg per nostril to a maximum of 4 mg. Titrating beyond that is a paramedic function.

quiz.q: Which statement about the June 24, 2024 NJ EMT scope waiver is correct?
choices: It authorizes EMTs to establish vascular access
It replaced N.J.A.C. 8:40A with a new chapter
It applies to every certified NJ EMT automatically
It permits approved BLS services to add albuterol, CPAP, PEEP valves and glucometers
quiz.why: The waiver names exactly those four items and grants relief agency by agency after an application to OEMS. It does not act on individual EMTs, add vascular access, or amend the code.

quiz.q: A semiconscious diabetic patient cannot follow commands and has a weak gag. Family offers glucose gel. What does NJ protocol require?
choices: Withhold oral glucose; the patient must be alert enough to swallow and protect the airway
Give glucose only after a glucometer reading
Give one tube slowly between the cheek and gum
Give two tubes to raise glucose faster
quiz.why: The hypoglycemia protocol conditions oral glucose on the patient being alert enough to swallow and protect the airway. Buccal placement in an obtunded patient still risks aspiration; call for ALS, who can give IV dextrose.

quiz.q: Which oxygen target does NJ protocol use for a stroke patient?
choices: Above 90%
100% by non-rebreather regardless of saturation
quiz.why: Protocol 2.23 sets SpO2 between 94% and 99% for symptomatic stroke patients. The 90% figure is the COPD allowance, and routine high-flow oxygen is not protocol.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old in pulmonary edema is spontaneously breathing, RR 32, SpO2 87%, with accessory muscle use and a BP of 148/90. Your agency is CPAP-approved. What is correct?
choices: Apply a nasal cannula at 4 L/min and reassess
Withhold CPAP because the respiratory rate is too high
Apply CPAP at 5 to 10 cm H2O and titrate to effect
Intubate
quiz.why: This patient meets every CPAP indication and has no contraindication; protocol 5.3 sets 5 to 10 cm H2O titrated to effect. Intubation is out of scope, a cannula is inadequate, and a high respiratory rate is an indication, not a contraindication.

quiz.q: Which of these is a NJ CPAP contraindication?
choices: History of COPD
Respiratory rate over 25
Oxygen saturation under 94%
Respiratory distress secondary to trauma
quiz.why: Distress from trauma is on the contraindication list, along with suspected pneumothorax, vomiting, apnea and SBP under 100. A rate over 25 and saturation under 94% are indications, and COPD is a qualifying condition.

quiz.q: Ten minutes into CPAP your patient becomes drowsy, the rate falls to 8, and saturation drops to 84%. What does NJ protocol direct?
choices: Discontinue CPAP and assist ventilations with a BVM
Continue CPAP and expedite transport
Increase pressure to 15 cm H2O
Add a nasal cannula under the mask
quiz.why: Protocol 5.3 step 11 says that if the patient deteriorates, discontinue CPAP and assist respirations by BVM. Raising pressure above 10 exceeds protocol, and continuing CPAP in a failing patient delays effective ventilation.

quiz.q: A conscious 46-year-old with an obvious Colles fracture is alert, oriented, with normal vitals, and refuses transport. What is the NJ-appropriate action?
choices: Transport against his will since the injury is deformed
Explain the specific risks, offer transport more than once, document a refusal with vitals and mental status
Call police to force transport
Have a family member sign for him
quiz.why: A competent adult may refuse. The defensible record is risk explanation in plain language, repeated offers, and documented vitals and mental status. Force is only for patients who are a danger to self or others.

quiz.q: A patient states he took an overdose intending to die but now refuses transport. He is alert and oriented. Under NJ protocol, what applies?
choices: He may refuse if a family member stays with him
He may refuse because he is alert and oriented
He may not refuse; contact police and the mental health crisis agency
Only a physician may override his refusal
quiz.why: The behavioral emergencies protocol states a patient who is a danger to self or others may not refuse care, and directs contacting police and, if available, the local mental health crisis agency. Orientation does not cure dangerousness.

quiz.q: A 16-year-old is struck by a car at a school event. No parent is reachable. What consent basis applies under NJ protocol 8.3?
choices: No care may be given until a guardian is located
A police officer must consent
The minor's own consent
Implied consent, with continued attempts to reach the parent
quiz.why: Protocol 8.3 allows treatment under implied consent when a parent or authorized representative is unavailable, while personnel attempt to reach the guardian except in life-threatening emergencies.

quiz.q: Which minor may refuse care in New Jersey?
choices: An emancipated minor who can establish emancipation
A minor whose friend confirms their maturity
A minor with a sports physical on file
Any minor over 16
quiz.why: Protocol 8.3 lists emancipated minors among the narrow exceptions, with the burden on the minor to establish emancipation. Age alone, peer testimony and medical paperwork are not exceptions.

quiz.q: An unresponsive patient wakes after your nasal naloxone and insists on staying home. What does the protocol say?
choices: He may refuse if fully oriented
Patients given naloxone should be transported to the ED for further evaluation
Give a second dose to confirm reversal, then release
Leave him with a family member and clear
quiz.why: The protocol directs transport of naloxone-treated patients for further evaluation, because naloxone can wear off before the opioid does and re-sedation is a real risk.

quiz.q: You arrive to find a pulseless 84-year-old and a copy, not the original, of a valid POLST directing DNAR. What do you do?
choices: Transport with CPR in progress and let the ED decide
Begin CPR because a copy is invalid
Follow the POLST; a copy of the original is considered valid
Begin CPR until police verify the document
quiz.why: Protocol 8.4 states a copy of the original POLST or Out-of-Hospital DNR is a valid document. Starting resuscitation against a valid order disregards a medical order.

quiz.q: A patient with a POLST marked DNAR is awake, talking, and says she now wants everything done. What governs?
choices: The surrogate's opinion
Medical command must decide before any care
The POLST, because it is a medical order
The patient's current wishes under standard consent procedures
quiz.why: Protocol 8.4 step 1 says the wishes of conscious and alert patients are followed under standard consent procedures. A form never overrides a patient who can speak for herself.

quiz.q: A POLST has Section B marked Limited Treatment with transfer only if comfort needs cannot be met on site, and the patient is in pain that you cannot relieve there. What is appropriate?
choices: Transport for comfort and symptom relief
Begin full resuscitative measures
Refuse the call as a non-emergency
Leave the patient at home regardless
quiz.why: Protocol 8.4 says Limited Treatment with that transfer condition means transport for comfort and symptom relief when comfort needs cannot be met in the current location. It is neither abandonment nor full treatment.

quiz.q: You cannot determine whether a DNR form is valid and the patient is in arrest. What is the safest correct action?
choices: Withhold resuscitation and call the medical examiner
Begin resuscitation and contact medical command
Ask the family to decide and follow their vote
Wait for police to authenticate the document
quiz.why: The default posture is full resuscitation, and the protocol directs contacting medical command when documentation is unclear. Starting is reversible; withholding is not, and family consensus is not a legal order.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old in Gloucester County has an unstable pelvis and hypotension after a high-speed crash. A community ED is 6 minutes away; Cooper is 22 minutes. What does NJ guidance support?
choices: Split the difference and go to the nearest Level II
Closest appropriate hospital always wins; go to the community ED
Transport to Cooper, the region's Level I trauma center, under the trauma system exception
Wait on scene for a helicopter regardless of weather
quiz.why: Protocol 1.0 states regionalized systems of care for trauma may necessitate transport to a specific facility, and 8.2 adopts national field triage. Cooper is the only Level I in South Jersey, and scene time should stay under 10 minutes.

quiz.q: Which hospital pair correctly lists South Jersey's state-designated trauma centers?
choices: Virtua Voorhees (Level I) and Inspira Vineland (Level II)
Cooper (Level II) and Jefferson Stratford (Level I)
AtlantiCare Mainland (Level I) and Shore Medical Center (Level II)
Cooper (Level I) and AtlantiCare City Campus (Level II)
quiz.why: The OEMS trauma center list shows Cooper in Camden at Level I and AtlantiCare Regional Medical Center City Campus at Level II. Virtua, Inspira, Jefferson and Shore are not on the designated trauma center list.

quiz.q: You perform B.E. F.A.S.T. on a 71-year-old with sudden right arm weakness and it is positive. What does NJ protocol 2.23 direct next?
choices: Perform a R.A.C.E. scale evaluation for large vessel occlusion
Wait for ALS to obtain a 12-lead
Give aspirin 324 mg
Transport immediately without further assessment
quiz.why: A positive B.E. F.A.S.T. triggers the R.A.C.E. scale, and a score above 5 prompts considering a Comprehensive Stroke Center. Aspirin is not a stroke intervention, and the protocol says not to delay for ALS.

quiz.q: No ALS is available for a 55-year-old with classic ACS symptoms, and transport to a cath-capable hospital is 16 minutes. What does NJ protocol 3.0 support?
choices: Transport to the closest hospital of any kind
Transport to an interventional cardiac catheterization capable hospital
Stay on scene until a medic is free
Request air medical transport routinely
quiz.why: Protocol 3.0 directs that if ALS is unavailable, transport to an interventional cath-capable hospital if greater than 10 minutes. Waiting on scene wastes myocardium and routine air transport is not indicated here.

quiz.q: You suspect abuse of a 4-year-old and report it at the ED to the charge nurse, who says she will handle it. Are you compliant with NJ requirements?
choices: Yes, hospital staff assume the duty at handoff
Yes, if you chart the conversation
No, the protocol says the provider must report directly
No, only a physician may report
quiz.why: Section 8.0 states the report should be made by the provider directly and that relying on another healthcare provider or law enforcement is inappropriate. N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.10 makes every person a reporter.

quiz.q: Which combination correctly pairs a NJ reporting duty with its destination?
choices: Both to the NJ Department of Health
Both to the receiving hospital's social work department
Suspected child abuse to the county prosecutor; vulnerable adult abuse to OEMS
Suspected child abuse to the State Central Registry at 1-877-NJ-ABUSE; vulnerable adult abuse to county Adult Protective Services
quiz.why: Child abuse goes to the State Central Registry at 1-877-NJ-ABUSE under N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.10; suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of a vulnerable adult goes to county Adult Protective Services under N.J.S.A. 52:27D-406 to 426.

quiz.q: Police handcuff a combative patient who needs transport for a head laceration. What does NJ protocol 6.5 require?
choices: The officer who applied the handcuffs must personally accompany the patient
Transport prone to prevent escape
Restraints may be applied without documentation if police are involved
Remove the handcuffs before moving the patient
quiz.why: Hard restraints such as handcuffs are prohibited unless the applying officer personally accompanies the patient. Prone positioning is never permitted, and restraint documentation is always required.

quiz.q: Under N.J.S.A. 30:4-27.5, what does a screening certificate authorize?
choices: Immediate involuntary medication
Detention without a court order for up to 72 hours while commitment proceedings begin
Permanent commitment
EMS transport against a competent patient's wishes for any complaint
quiz.why: A screening certificate executed by a mental health screener permits detention for no more than 72 hours, during which the facility must initiate involuntary commitment proceedings. It is not a treatment order or a permanent action.

quiz.q: A woman hands your crew a 3-day-old infant at the station and asks no questions be asked. What does NJ protocol 8.8 direct?
choices: Transport the infant and file a child abuse report
Refuse and call police to investigate
Accept the infant, protect anonymity, and call the Safe Haven hotline at 1-877-839-2339 no later than the first business day
Demand identification before accepting
quiz.why: The NJ Safe Haven Infant Protection Act permits anonymous surrender at an ambulance squad; the protocol directs calling 1-877-839-2339 no later than the first business day and preserving anonymity. Demanding ID defeats the law's purpose.

quiz.q: Which is required for New Jersey PA licensure?
choices: Two years of supervised clinical practice before licensure
NREMT paramedic certification
A doctoral degree and state jurisprudence exam only
An ARC-PA accredited program plus passing the NCCPA examination
quiz.why: N.J.A.C. 13:35-2B.5 requires graduation from an ARC-PA accredited program and a passing NCCPA exam score, plus being 18 and of good moral character. No doctorate or pre-licensure practice period is required.

quiz.q: How does New Jersey structure physician assistant practice authority?
choices: Physician-delegated scope under continuous supervision with a written delegation agreement
Collaboration only, with no written agreement required
Practice limited to hospital settings
Full independent practice after licensure
quiz.why: The Physician Assistant Licensing Act creates a physician-delegated scope: the service must be delegated, within the PA's skills, and a component of the physician's scope, under supervision documented by an annually signed delegation agreement.

quiz.q: A NJ PA wants to initiate a new Schedule II prescription for a patient. What does the statute require?
choices: Nothing beyond the PA's own DEA registration
Physician authorization to prescribe CDS, DEA registration, the DEA number printed on the order, and prior consultation with the supervising physician
A separate Board waiver for each prescription
That the physician personally examine the patient first
quiz.why: N.J.S.A. 45:9-27.19 permits initiating a CDS order only with physician authorization and prior consultation, and the PA must be DEA registered and print the DEA number on the order. Continuing an existing order and adjusting doses have their own conditions.

quiz.q: How many continuing education credits does a NJ PA need per renewal period, and how long is that period?
choices: 25 credits every 12 months
48 credits over 36 months
50 Category I credits every 24 months
100 credits every 24 months
quiz.why: N.J.A.C. 13:35-2B.7 and 2B.8 set biennial renewal with 50 Category I credits, including one opioid-prescribing credit. The 48-over-36-months figure is the EMT recertification rule.

quiz.q: A 2022 article says NJ PAs may practice without a delegation agreement due to an executive order. Is that still accurate?
choices: Yes, but only in hospitals
No; NJ never waived the requirement
Yes, the waivers were made permanent
No; the COVID-era waivers ended at 5:00 PM on April 2, 2026 and statutory supervision applies again
quiz.why: Executive Order 415 of January 16, 2026 terminated the waivers and, after an extension under Executive Order 13, they expired at 5:00 PM on April 2, 2026. PAs are again subject to statutory supervision and delegation agreements.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 74F, difficulty breathing, Deptford
scenarios.intro:
You are the EMT on a BLS unit in Gloucester County. Your service is approved under the OEMS expanded scope for albuterol, CPAP, PEEP valves and glucometry. Dispatch: 74-year-old female, difficulty breathing, second floor of a single-family home. ALS is committed on another call with an estimated 14 minutes to you. The nearest emergency department is 7 minutes away.

She is sitting bolt upright on the edge of the bed, tripoding, speaking in three-word sentences. Her ankles are swollen and you hear crackles from the doorway.

steps.prompt: You are at her side. She is anxious, diaphoretic, and pulling with her neck muscles on every breath. Her husband says she has heart failure and takes a water pill.

choices.text: Sit her fully upright, apply pulse oximetry, and prepare CPAP while your partner requests ALS intercept
choices.feedback: Correct. She meets every CPAP indication in protocol 5.3: spontaneously breathing, moderate to severe distress from pulmonary edema, SpO2 under 94%, accessory muscle use, and a rate over 25. Preparing while calling for ALS wastes no time.

choices.text: Lay her flat to make bag valve mask ventilation easier
choices.feedback: Harmful. Supine worsens pulmonary edema by increasing venous return to an already overloaded heart, and she is still breathing on her own. The NJ asthma and CHF protocols both direct a position of comfort, usually upright.

choices.text: Apply a nasal cannula at 4 L/min and reassess in five minutes
choices.feedback: Inadequate. A cannula will not move a saturation of 86% in a patient with this much work of breathing, and five minutes of watching is five minutes lost.

choices.text: Assist with her prescribed nitroglycerin
choices.feedback: Not supported. NJ protocol authorizes assisting with the patient's own nitroglycerin under the acute coronary syndrome protocol for chest pain, not as a heart failure treatment at the EMT level.

steps.prompt: You explain the mask and coach her through it. Before you seat it, your partner reports the blood pressure again and asks what pressure you want.

choices.text: Start at 5 cm H2O and titrate upward within the 5 to 10 cm H2O range to effect
choices.feedback: Correct. Protocol 5.3 sets 5 to 10 cm H2O adjusted to effect. Starting low and climbing improves tolerance, which matters because a patient who rips the mask off gets no benefit at all.

choices.text: Start at 15 cm H2O for maximum benefit
choices.feedback: Out of protocol. The NJ range stops at 10 cm H2O. Higher pressures increase gastric insufflation and drop preload further.

choices.text: Skip CPAP; her systolic is high so she does not need it
choices.feedback: Wrong reasoning. Hypotension under 100 systolic is the contraindication. A systolic of 162 is reassuring for CPAP, not a reason to withhold it.

choices.text: Apply CPAP but hold the mask loosely by hand rather than strapping it
choices.feedback: Partially reasonable for the first 30 seconds of coaching, but the protocol directs securing the mask with straps until there is minimal air leak. A held mask leaks and never reaches set pressure.

steps.prompt: Eight minutes in, she is calmer, speaking in short sentences, and the neck muscles are quieter.

choices.text: Maintain CPAP for the duration of transport and notify the receiving hospital to prepare for a CPAP patient
choices.feedback: Correct. Protocol 5.3 step 10 says exactly this. Pulling the mask because she looks better is how patients crash in the ED parking lot.

choices.text: Remove CPAP now that saturation is 94% and switch to a non-rebreather
choices.feedback: Premature. The improvement is the CPAP working. Removing it returns her to the physiology that got her to 86%.

choices.text: Stay on scene until the medic arrives since she is improving
choices.feedback: No. She is improving on a treatment you can continue in the truck, and the ED is 7 minutes away. Waiting adds risk without adding capability.

steps.prompt: You are two minutes from the emergency department. Your partner asks what needs to be in the chart.

choices.text: Document the CPAP procedure, the time applied, the provider, and serial pulse oximetry readings showing the effect
choices.feedback: Correct, and it is a protocol requirement, not a preference. Protocol 5.3 step 12 names the time, the provider, and serial oximetry as the record that demonstrates the treatment worked.

choices.text: Document only the final vital signs, since those are what the ED will use
choices.feedback: Insufficient. A single set of vitals cannot show the trajectory, and the protocol specifically calls for serial readings.

choices.text: Chart the CPAP as an ALS assist since a medic was requested
choices.feedback: Inaccurate. CPAP is the only approved BLS adjunct in New Jersey, and you performed it under your agency's expanded-scope approval. Charting it as ALS misrepresents who did what.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: NJ CPAP is a checklist, not a judgment call. Indications are three findings plus a qualifying condition, contraindications are eight named items with hypotension under 100 systolic as the one that catches people, pressure lives between 5 and 10 cm H2O, improvement means keep it on and pre-notify, and deterioration means take it off and bag. Every step you take on a CPAP patient has a documentation partner: time, provider, and serial oximetry. Note also what did not happen here. You never waited for ALS to start a treatment that was already yours, because the protocol's call for intercept is a request, not a pause.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 19M, unresponsive, apartment in Camden
scenarios.intro:
You are dispatched for an unresponsive male. Police are on scene. A roommate says he found him in the bathroom about five minutes ago and that he uses fentanyl. The roommate is 17 and frightened, and there is a 2-year-old asleep in the next room.

The patient is supine on the bathroom floor, cyanotic around the lips, with slow shallow respirations. ALS is 9 minutes out. Your agency carries naloxone nasal spray in the 4 mg formulation.

steps.prompt: You kneel down. He does not respond to a sternal rub. Respirations are about 5 per minute and shallow. Pupils are pinpoint.

choices.text: Open the airway with an NPA and begin BVM ventilation with 100% oxygen, then give naloxone 4 mg nasal spray
choices.feedback: Correct and in the right order. Protocol 2.3A puts manual ventilation via BVM with 100% oxygen and a nasopharyngeal airway first, then the naloxone. Oxygen fixes the thing that kills him; naloxone fixes the cause.

choices.text: Give naloxone 4 mg nasal spray immediately and wait for him to breathe
choices.feedback: Incomplete. Naloxone takes minutes to work through the nasal mucosa, and at RR 5 with SpO2 79% he cannot wait. The NJ protocol ventilates first.

choices.text: Apply a non-rebreather at 15 L/min and monitor
choices.feedback: Harmful. A non-rebreather delivers oxygen but does not move air. A patient breathing 5 times a minute needs ventilation, not just a higher oxygen concentration.

choices.text: Begin chest compressions
choices.feedback: Not indicated. He has a pulse at 58. Compressions on a perfusing patient are inappropriate; ventilate instead.

steps.prompt: Three minutes later he is breathing on his own at 16 and opens his eyes. He sits up angrily, says he is fine, and tells you to get out.

choices.text: Explain that NJ protocol directs transport after naloxone, assess his capacity, and keep offering transport
choices.feedback: Correct. The protocol states patients given naloxone should be transported for further evaluation, because naloxone can wear off before the fentanyl does. Assessing capacity and repeating the offer is the right process even if he ultimately refuses.

choices.text: Accept his refusal immediately and clear the scene
choices.feedback: Too fast. He was unresponsive three minutes ago, the drug's duration may outlast the antidote, and you have not assessed present capacity or explained the specific risk of re-sedation.

choices.text: Tell police to handcuff him and force transport
choices.feedback: Not supported on these facts. Force is reserved for a patient who is a danger to self or others. Hard restraints require the applying officer to accompany the patient, and this is not the first tool to reach for.

choices.text: Check a blood glucose and reassess mental status before accepting any refusal
choices.feedback: Reasonable if your agency is approved for glucometry. Correcting reversible causes of altered mentation before judging capacity is exactly right, though ventilation and the naloxone conversation come first.

steps.prompt: He agrees to transport after you explain the risk of re-sedation. While packaging, you notice the 2-year-old in the next room: the apartment has no food in it, the child is in a soiled diaper, and the 17-year-old roommate says he is the only one who ever feeds her.

choices.text: Report the child's condition yourself to the State Central Registry at 1-877-NJ-ABUSE and document the report
choices.feedback: Correct. N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.10 makes every person a mandated reporter with reasonable cause, and NJ protocol 8.0 states the report must be made by the provider directly. You do not need proof.

choices.text: Mention it to the ED nurse and let the hospital report it
choices.feedback: Not sufficient. Section 8.0 says relying on another healthcare provider or on law enforcement to make the report is inappropriate. Your duty is personal.

choices.text: Confront the roommate about who is responsible for the child before deciding
choices.feedback: Do not do this. The protocol explicitly warns against confronting suspected perpetrators; it creates danger for you and for the patient, and the reporting decision does not require an investigation.

choices.text: Note the observations in your report and call the registry from the hospital before clearing
choices.feedback: Acceptable. The duty is to report immediately, and completing the call before you clear meets the intent, though earlier is better if a crew member is free.

steps.prompt: En route, the patient becomes drowsy again. He is rousable to voice, respirations 10 and shallow, SpO2 91%. You are 6 minutes from the emergency department and the ALS unit is now available.

choices.text: Assist ventilations with a BVM, repeat naloxone per protocol, and request the ALS intercept while continuing toward the ED
choices.feedback: Correct. The protocol permits repeating the initial naloxone dose after 5 minutes, ventilation remains the priority, and continuing transport while ALS comes to you loses nothing.

choices.text: Pull over and wait on the shoulder for the medic before doing anything
choices.feedback: No. Stopping delays definitive care for a treatment you can already deliver. The protocol repeatedly directs against delaying transport.

choices.text: Give a third and fourth naloxone spray back to back to stay ahead of it
choices.feedback: Beyond EMT protocol. The NJ EMT dose is the initial spray, repeatable once after 5 minutes, or 1 mg per nostril to a maximum of 4 mg. Titrating further is a paramedic function.

scenarios.debrief: Three New Jersey patterns collide in this call. First, oxygenation precedes the antidote: protocol 2.3A ventilates with a BVM and an NPA before naloxone, because hypoxia is what kills an opioid overdose. Second, naloxone creates a refusal problem by design, and the protocol answers it in advance by directing transport for further evaluation; when the patient re-sedated en route, that instruction proved itself. Third, your legal duties do not wait for a quiet moment. New Jersey makes every person a child abuse reporter, and the protocol says the report comes from you, not from the hospital or the police. The habit worth building is to notice the scene while you treat the patient, then make the call yourself and write down that you did.
